meta.cite: Barton O. Oliver's mTOR Atlas (live data, not an archived version; give corpus_snapshot and source_commit). doi:10.5281/zenodo.22059963

data.mechanism: Glutamine burned through glutaminolysis raises alpha-ketoglutarate, which promotes RagB GTP loading and mTORC1 translocation to the lysosome. This edge asserts the Rag-dependent route only.
data.mechanism_beginner: Glutamine can switch on mTORC1 partly just by being burned for fuel: burning it makes a molecule that helps the Rag proteins pull mTORC1 to the lysosome.
data.boundary: Cell-type dependent, and deliberately narrow: the separate claim that glutamine can reach mTORC1 without the Rags is carried by its own edge rather than folded in here.

conflict.basis: The two studies asked the same question - is glutamine's activation of mTORC1 Rag-dependent? - and answered it oppositely in comparable systems. DUR2012 reports that glutamine, with leucine, acts through glutaminolysis and alpha-ketoglutarate upstream of the Rags: inhibiting glutaminolysis prevented RagB GTP loading and lysosomal translocation of mTORC1, and a constitutively active Rag heterodimer activated mTORC1 without glutaminolysis. JEW2015 reports that glutamine promoted mTORC1 translocation in RagA and RagB knockout cells, requiring the v-ATPase and Arf1 but not Ragulator. Both are mammalian cell work, so this is a head-to-head disagreement rather than two different contexts. The Atlas carries the two routes as separate edges (this one and GLN-MTORC1-ARF1), each listing the other's study as conflicting, and does not settle whether they act in parallel or in different settings.

data.note: Split from the Rag-independent claim on 2026-09-13 after external review: one edge was asserting a Rag-dependent mechanism and describing a Rag-independent one in the same sentence. 2026-10-10: this edge's curation status (Contested) and its field consensus (emerging) deliberately differ, and the evidence-audit page now labels the two dimensions separately instead of presenting either count as the number of disputed claims.
